comparison: Both evaluate the core fMRI findings on pRF size changes (C2, C3, C61-C67, C70-C71, C86-C87, C121-C122). OpenEval finds the evidence SUPPORTED with appropriate statistical methods and robustness across areas, acknowledging variability in higher visual areas. Peer review rates this UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 2 expressing major concerns about statistical rigor, reproducibility, and significance boundaries, particularly questioning effects beyond V2. This represents a significant disagreement on the strength of the neuroimaging evidence.

Both address visual inspection of pRF maps (C61). OpenEval considers this part of converging evidence supporting the claims. Peer review explicitly challenges this as UNSUPPORTED, with Reviewer 2 stating they disagree that differences are 'clear' and suggesting the visualization method is inadequate. This is a direct disagreement on the interpretability of the visual data.

Both evaluate psychophysical aftereffect findings (C42-C44, C51, C84-C85). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with emphasis on statistical significance and appropriate controls. Peer review also rates SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 3 confirming the study is 'well-designed' and Reviewer 1 noting satisfactory data quality. Strong agreement on the behavioral findings.

Both evaluate the contrast control experiment (C81, C102). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting the null result effectively rules out contrast confounds though Bayesian evidence is only moderate. Peer review also rates SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 3 explicitly acknowledging this control without challenge. Strong agreement on this methodological control.

Both evaluate the main conclusion linking SF selectivity to pRF size (C1, C26, C82, C88, C123). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED based on convergence of psychophysical and neuroimaging evidence. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN, acknowledging the importance and novelty but noting the conclusion's strength depends on the contested fMRI results, particularly Reviewer 2's concerns about statistical significance beyond V2. Disagreement on whether evidence sufficiently supports the central claim.

Both evaluate fixation compliance evidence (C72). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting high response rates support attention though this is indirect. Peer review also rates SUPPORTED without challenge. Agreement on this methodological detail.

Minimal overlap on C50 (hemifield pooling control). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, referencing appendix analysis. Peer review includes C50 in their evaluation of psychophysical findings rated SUPPORTED. Both accept this control without specific discussion.

OpenEval evaluates SNR similarity between conditions (C101) as SUPPORTED, noting this rules out SNR confounds. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though this addresses a potential methodological concern.

OpenEval rates claims about brief adaptation effectiveness in fMRI (C97, C99-C100) as UNCERTAIN, noting the accumulation hypothesis is plausible but not directly measured. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval evaluates asymmetry in aftereffects (C104-C106) as SUPPORTED with appropriate literature citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval rates contextualization with prior literature on pRF vs single-unit RF (C89-C91) as SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval evaluates discussion of contradictory prior work (C92-C96) as SUPPORTED, finding explanations plausible though speculative. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval rates speculative implications for other perceptual phenomena (C107-C120) as UNCERTAIN, noting these are hypotheses rather than tested predictions. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval evaluates standard methodological details (C35-C60, C78) as SUPPORTED for reproducibility. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though these are typically accepted without explicit comment.

OpenEval rates literature citations and theoretical grounding (C4-C33, C76, C103) as SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers typically do not systematically evaluate citation accuracy.
